Biden eyes adding AI chip curbs to Chinese companies abroad
In the initial round of curbs, the Biden administration left overseas subsidiaries of Chinese companies with unfettered access to the same semiconductors, meaning they could easily be smuggled into China or accessed remotely by China-based users.
By Alexandra Alper and Karen Freifeld
The Biden administration is considering closing a loophole that gives Chinese companies access to American artificial intelligence (AI) chips through units located overseas, according to four people familiar with the matter.
The United States last year shook relations with Beijing when it unveiled new restrictions on shipments of AI chips and chipmaking tools to China, seeking to thwart its military advances. Those rules are set to be tightened in the coming days. A person familiar with the situation said the measure could be included in those new restrictions.
In the initial round of curbs, the Biden administration left overseas subsidiaries of Chinese companies with unfettered access to the same semiconductors, meaning they could easily be smuggled into China or accessed remotely by China-based users.
Reuters reported in June that the very chips barred by U.S. regulations could be purchased from vendors in the famed Huaqiangbei electronics area in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen.
Washington is now mulling ways to close the loophole, sources said, a move that has not been previously reported.
The efforts to close the loophole show how the Biden administration is struggling to cut China off from top AI technology and how difficult it is to plug every gap in export controls.
"Absolutely, Chinese firms are purchasing chips for use in data centers abroad," said Greg Allen, a director at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, noting that Singapore is a big hub for cloud computing.
The Commerce Department declined to comment. A representative from the Chinese Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment. China's Ministry of Commerce has previously accused the U.S. of abusing export controls and called for it to "stop its unreasonable suppression of Chinese companies."
While it would be illegal under U.S. law to ship those AI chips to mainland China, it is very difficult for the United States to police those transactions, experts said, noting that China-based employees could legally access the chips located at foreign subsidiaries remotely as well.
"We don't actually know how big a problem this is," said Hanna Dohmen, a Research Analyst at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET).
The United States has been seeking to halt the rise of China's artificial intelligence capability, which helps its military develop unmanned combat systems, according to a report in The International Affairs Review, affiliated with George Washington University's School of International Affairs.
China's AI capability depends on its access to U.S. chips. CSET found in a June 2022 report that out of 97 individual AI chips procured via Chinese military tenders over an 8-month period in 2020, nearly all of them were designed by U.S.-based companies Nvidia, Xilinx, Intel, and Microsemi.
Washington has been working to close other loopholes that allow the AI chips into China. In August, it told Nvidia and AMD to restrict shipments of the AI chips beyond China to other regions, including some countries in the Middle East.
Sources said the new rules on AI chips expected this month will likely apply those same restrictions more broadly to all companies in the market.
It is less clear how the U.S. government might close the loophole allowing Chinese parties to access U.S. cloud providers like Amazon Web Services, which give their customers access to the same AI capabilities. But sources say the Biden administration is grappling with that issue as well.
"Chinese persons can completely legally access the same chips from anywhere in the world. There are no rules about how they can be accessed," said Timothy Fist, a fellow at Washington-based think tank Center for a New American Security.

BEIJING: China has published proposed security requirements for firms offering services powered by generative artificial intelligence, including a blacklist of sources that cannot be used to train AI models.
Generative AI, popularised by the success of OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot, learns how to take actions from past data, and creates new content like text or images based on that training.
The requirements were published on Wednesday by the National Information Security Standardization Committee, which includes officials from the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC), the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, and the police.
The committee proposes conducting a security assessment of each body of content used to train public-facing generative AI models, with those containing "more than 5% of illegal and harmful information" to be blacklisted.
Such information includes "advocating terrorism" or violence, as well as "overthrowing the socialist system", "damaging the country's image", and "undermining national unity and social stability".
The draft rules also state that information censored on the Chinese internet should not be used to train models.
Its publication comes just over a month after regulators allowed several Chinese tech firms, including search engine giant Baidu, to launch their generative AI-driven chatbots to the public.
The CAC has since April said it wanted firms to submit security assessments to authorities before launching generative AI-driven services to the public.
In July, the cyberspace regulator published measures governing such services that analysts said were far less onerous than measures outlined in an April draft.
The draft security requirements published on Wednesday require organisations training these AI models to seek the consent of individuals whose personal information, including biometric data, is used for training purposes.
They also lay out detailed guidelines on how to avoid intellectual property violations.
Countries globally are grappling with setting guardrails for the technology. China sees AI as an area in which it wants to rival the U.S, and has set it sights on becoming a world leader in the field by 2030.

text:
- Internet
- 1 min read
Google to defend generative AI users from copyright claims
Major technology companies like Google have been investing heavily in generative AI and racing to incorporate it into their products. Prominent writers, illustrators and other copyright owners have said in several lawsuits that both the use of their work to train the AI systems and the content the systems create violate their rights.
By Blake Brittain
Google said on Thursday that it will defend users of generative artificial-intelligence systems in its Google Cloud and Workspace platforms if they are accused of intellectual property violations, joining Microsoft , Adobe and other companies that have made similar pledges.
Major technology companies like Google have been investing heavily in generative AI and racing to incorporate it into their products. Prominent writers, illustrators and other copyright owners have said in several lawsuits that both the use of their work to train the AI systems and the content the systems create violate their rights.
"To our knowledge, Google is the first in the industry to offer a comprehensive, two-pronged approach to indemnity" that specifically covers both types of claims, a company spokesperson said.
Google said its new policy applies to software, including its Vertex AI development platform and Duet AI system, which generates text and images in Google Workspace and Cloud programs. The press release did not mention Google's more well-known generative AI chatbot program Bard.
The company also said the indemnity does not apply if users "intentionally create or use generated output to infringe the rights of others."
The new wave of lawsuits over generative AI has generally targeted the companies that own the systems, including Google, and not individual end users.
AI defendants have said that the use of training data scraped from the internet to train their systems qualifies as fair use under U.S. copyright law.

title: US military needs AI vehicles, weapon systems to be 'superior' global force: experts
text:
Retired Army Gen. Mark Milley believes that artificial intelligence will be a critical component of keeping the U.S. military one step ahead of potential adversaries.
"Our military is going to have to change if we are going to continue to be superior to every other military on Earth," Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said during an interview with "60 Minutes" this week.
According to Milley, future wars will look drastically different with the seemingly rapid development of AI technology, something the U.S. will have to be prepared for and adopt if they want to win future wars.
US, NOT CHINA, SHOULD TAKE LEAD ON AI
"Artificial intelligence is extremely powerful," Milley said. "It's coming at us. I suspect it will be probably optimized for command and control of military operations within maybe 10 to 15 years, max."
That sentiment is shared by Christopher Alexander, a former Army information warfare operations operator and current chief analytics officer of Pioneer Development Group, who told Fox News Digital that the technology will be useful to military planners in more ways than one.
"AI is crucial for a range of different functions in the military. From autonomous vehicles to intelligence analysis, AI will help make more of existing resources," Alexander said, adding that such technology will allow "planners and analysts to be freed from more monotonous tasks to focus on higher-order thinking."
"At the core of all of these capabilities is the ability of AI to expedite the understanding of difficult circumstances and rapidly respond with precision strike capabilities," Alexander said. "This will transfer from staff processes all the way to the battlefield."
Milley told "60 Minutes" that one specific area where AI will do this is with the "OODA loop" (observe, orient, decide, act) with military leaders constantly attempting to determine the next course of action to outmaneuver their enemy. In the past, Milley said, such a strategy would have seen Napoleon waking up in the middle of the night to issue orders before the British had morning tea, but in the future, AI will be used to analyze large chunks of information and give suggestions on where and when to move U.S. forces.
"This is a perfect example of where AI and war gaming can intersect to set strategy and tactics," Phil Siegel, founder of the Center for Advanced Preparedness and Threat Response Simulation, told Fox News Digital. "There are so many options for using AI, from autonomous vehicles to troop and equipment placement, to consumables usage and replenishment, to simply providing input on battle strategy and tactics. Gaming which uses will be most advantageous and have the best payoff will allow the military to invest wisely in the technology."
Siegel noted that it will be important for the military to hire "solid AI experts" and have solid relationships "with the private sector," something that would "allow the military to accelerate its capabilities."
"Everyone is already using AI technologies and will be accelerating their use," Siegel said. "Our military needs to invest heavily to stay out front."

Like Siegel, Milley says every country will have access to and use AI technology in military operations, making it critical for the U.S. to stay at the forefront of the changing landscape.
But when asked if such technology could lead to wars becoming more likely, Milley said such implications are something that leaders are still trying to "come to grips with."
"It could. It actually could," Milley said. "Artificial intelligence has a huge amount of legal, ethical and moral implications that we're just beginning to start to come to grips with."

title: AI Could Be Apple’s Next Chapter
text:
After Nvidia added $750 billion in value this year on the backs of surging AI chip demand, investors are quickly searching for the next trillion-dollar AI winner. AI is the best investment opportunity of our lifetimes, and although Apple (AAPL) has been relatively overlooked as an AI play, the tech giant could quickly become a force to be reckoned with in the AI space. The reason for this is simple, Apple (AAPL) can bring AI to the consumer’s pocket by the billions, and is rumored to be sitting on one of the best AI models on the market today with comparable performance as OpenAI’s ChatGPT.
Two Billion Devices to Lever AI
Apple’s installed active device base surpassed 2 billion in February this year, and “reached an all-time high in every geographic segment” at the end of the June quarter, according to comments from CFO Luca Maestri. The iPhone’s installed base also “grew to a new all-time high,” and is estimated to have nearly 1.5 billion active devices worldwide, after adding around 500 million active devices since 2019 – an 11.4% CAGR since then.
While installed active devices reached a new record, so did Apple’s subscriber base. CEO Tim Cook noted during Apple’s FQ3 report in August that the company hit an “all-time revenue record in Services” with “over 1 billion paid subscriptions,” which are growing at a double-digit rate. Apple has added more than 65 million subscribers in the first half of this fiscal year, and more than 300 million subscribers over the past two fiscal years heading into its fiscal Q4.
The opportunity for Apple to capitalize on AI arises from the combination of growth within Apple’s installed device base, along with increased engagement and adoption of paid subscriptions over time. Consumer interest in AI surged earlier in 2023 with ChatGPT garnering over 100 million active users and more than 1 billion visits monthly. Apple’s installed base offers the chance to more than 10x the number of individuals with readily available access to AI.
Services Is Where AI Can Shine
Apple is witnessing a higher contribution from its Services segment to both revenues and margins – the segment is approaching a $100 billion annual run rate, accounting for nearly 26% of revenue with a 70.5% gross margin.
In other words, Services is contributing 41.1 cents to each dollar of gross profit, up from 34.6 cents just eight quarters ago. The segment has seen its contribution to gross profit increase steadily, rising 46% from 23.7 cents per dollar in FY18 to 34.6 cents per dollar to date in FY23. It is not out of the picture for Services to soon contribute 50 cents of each dollar of gross profit as the segment surpasses $100 billion in annual revenue.
The importance of Services to Apple’s bottom line cannot be overstated – that 70% gross margin level combined with its nearly $100 billion revenue scale has pulled Apple’s margins higher over the past few years, and will likely continue to do so in the future as transacting accounts and paid accounts continue to grow to new all-time highs.
This is exactly where AI will have the most profound impact on Apple, and why the tech giant could emerge as a strong AI contender.
Google and Microsoft demonstrate the revenue potential of AI subscriptions at scale – for Microsoft’s Copilot, a 2.5% take rate of the ~382 million commercial Office 365 users would equate to nearly $3.5 billion in annual revenue, while a 10% take rate would see annual revenue reaching $14 billion, according to Macquarie.
In Apple’s case, it has nearly three times the paid subscription base as Microsoft that it could target with an AI product, via a stand-alone service or in one of its three pre-existing service bundles. Regardless of the route that Apple chooses, there remains billions in revenue potential. Offering a stand-alone AI subscription for $2.99 per month could rake in ~$10.8 billion in annual revenue at a 15% attach rate based on Apple’s more than 2 billion active devices, while boosting the prices of its subscription bundles could by $0.50 per month could add more than $5 billion annually.
Apple Can Bridge the Gap with Mass-Market Consumer AI
Apple is spending millions of dollars per day in a quest to develop a conversational AI model, potentially for Siri, that would allow iPhone and iPad owners to use voice commands for automating multi-step tasks with the voice assistant. As such, Apple is uniquely positioned to both monetize and implement advanced AI in a mass-market consumer application.
Consumers, especially Millennials, are very willing to adopt and pay for such voice assistants that are as smart and as reliable as a human. According to a PYMNTS survey from April, more than 42% are willing to pay $10 or more per month for an assistant.
Although Apple is tight-lipped about the progress of its AI projects, the so-called Apple GPT chatbot is rumored to be more powerful than Open AI’s GPT 3.5 model, according to The Verge. Apple is spending millions of dollars a day training the large language model Ajax on more than 200 billion parameters.
The project could find life integrated within Siri, given the applications within automating multiple tasks and range of capabilities stemming from image and video recognition.
Apple noted back in 2020 that Siri had more than 25 billion requests made per month, a figure that could easily be increased with a ChatGPT-like chatbot installed across billions of devices. That is how Apple can be the first big stock in consumer driven AI uptake.
On Real Vision, I previously pointed out that “if you take a consumer-facing company like Google,” that they are in a good position because Google doesn’t “have to go out and try to get lots of consumers to adopt something new, consumers will continue to use Search, it’ll just be improved Search; advertisers will continue to use Google, it’ll just be improved ROI.”
For Apple, it’s the same case – it does not have to try to convert millions of users into a paid subscriber in the way that OpenAI does; rather, it could easily integrate an advanced conversational AI model within Siri for example, and quickly convert already-paying subscribers over to those AI services.

title: Council Post: Beyond Law Firms: How Legal Tech's Real Frontier Lies With SMBs
text:
By Charles Brecque, CEO and Founder of Legislate.
Data and artificial intelligence are transforming the legal technology space—there’s no doubt about it. A recent Thomson Reuters Institute survey of lawyers showed that a large majority (82%) of respondents believe ChatGPT and generative AI can be readily applied to legal work.
While it's tempting to think of legal tech as a playground exclusive to law firms, as technology enables employees without legal training to use and create legal frameworks and documentation, I’d like to challenge that narrative. Being the founder of a company that uses AI to manage contracts, the way I see it is the real magic happens when legal tech tools meet the day-to-day challenges of small and medium-sized businesses (known as "SMBs").
But why SMBs?
At first glance, law and SMBs might seem disconnected, but at the heart of every business are contracts. Contracts define collaborations, seal deals and are the backbone of commerce. Yet, for many SMBs, managing these contracts with suppliers or customers can be complex and tedious, especially with limited legal resources, as most SMBs can’t afford to invest in big legal departments.
Enter large language models as applied to legal tech. With LLMs, we're not just talking about a smart tool that can decode legal jargon, though that's certainly a part of it. We're talking about a legal copilot that can generate, analyze search and optimize contracts in real-time. Beyond conserving time and resources, LLMs can reveal intricate patterns in contracts, highlight specific traits in the most beneficial agreements, pinpoint contracts that endure prolonged negotiations and discern terms that regularly face challenges or neglect.
By tapping into the capabilities of LLMs, SMBs can not only transform their approach to contract management but also refine business decisions related to their sales efforts.
Nothing good comes without challenges.
Like all good things, bringing LLMs into SMB legal tech doesn't happen without its challenges. For businesses to successfully implement and put their own models to use for contract management purposes, there are a few considerations to take into account.
Solving The Hosting Hurdle
LLMs demand a lot in terms of infrastructure. One question for SMBs is whether to lean on third-party cloud solutions or invest in their own machinery. Data privacy, coupled with the costs of hosting models on graphics processing units, makes this a critical decision point. Here, solutions provided by companies that offer a way to compress LLMs can help improve how businesses implement, maintain and manage them.
Navigating Integration And Usability
Integrating LLMs into SMBs’ contract management workflows has consequences, particularly in terms of the employee adoption of these models. Leaders need to understand how the LLMs will be used across the organization—be it by the legal team or another department. The experience and background of these users will determine whether they can judge LLMs' output appropriately.
Choosing a legal tool or provider that doesn't offer excessive freedom in prompt selection is one way to help mitigate potential errors or "hallucinations." If, however, you're developing your own model, it's essential to ensure that users are trained to recognize unreliable outputs. A useful tip is to always ask the LLM for the source of its response. If it can't provide one or cites an incorrect source, it's likely hallucinating.
Second, SMBs need to think about LLMs’ compatibility with their current technology and their in-house expertise—and factor in the time to adapt. Each LLM can have distinct architectural requirements. While most software operates on central processing units (or "CPUs), LLMs typically need GPUs. These not only come at a higher cost but also function differently from CPUs. As a result, IT teams might face a learning curve if they're not familiar with GPU-based tools.
Finally, it’ll be important to bear in mind the impact on the SMBs’ various stakeholders. There might be varied responses to the adoption of LLMs, and transparency and clear communication are key. Highlighting the benefits of the new tech while also addressing potential concerns ensures all parties remain aligned and comfortable. SMBs can do this easily by creating a code of conduct or LLM guidelines that are openly shared with their stakeholders.
Understanding The Data Privacy Trade-Off
As LLMs develop, they constantly refine their models using incoming data. For SMBs that hold personal or proprietary information in contracts and other legal documents, this is an important decision. Do you provide the LLM with data to boost its efficiency, potentially risking IP exposure to third parties? If you do and you're working with a legal tech provider, ask whether it operates an LLM on its own secure servers. Similarly, if you work with an LLM provider, ask whether it has an enterprise package that prioritizes enhanced privacy safeguards.
How can SMBs effectively add LLMs to their legal tech arsenal?
For those SMBs looking to adopt LLMs, here are three tips.
1. Identify the use case. Start with clarity. Determine precisely where and how an LLM can benefit your operations. It's not about having the tech for tech's sake but about leveraging it for tangible outcomes.
2. Reflect on your data stance. If you’re not comfortable sharing your data on external clouds, look inward. Building in-house might be more intensive initially, but it ensures control.
3. Anticipate the change. Make sure you’re aware of what this adoption will mean for your company, employees and stakeholders. Put together a roadmap and internal guidelines before you activate it to ensure a smooth rollout.
It's an exciting era for SMBs. While the initial hurdles in adopting LLMs might put leaders off, the long-term benefits are well worth the effort. This isn't about jumping onto the latest tech bandwagon. It's about understanding the specific needs of the business, appreciating the potential pitfalls and leveraging technology for meaningful, tangible outcomes. As with any tool, it's not about possession but application.

title: Council Post: Navigating Ethical AI And The Future Of Automation
text:
Vamsi Krishna Gosu - Founder & Director, TechForce Services.
In today's fast-paced world, we find ourselves at the intersection of technology and humanity, where artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are reshaping the way we live and work. These advancements hold incredible potential, promising to simplify tasks, enhance accuracy and redefine our experiences. Yet, as we journey through this transformative landscape, we must pause to consider a fundamental question: How can we ensure that our embrace of AI is guided by ethical principles?
At TechForce Services, as a Salesforce consulting firm, we partner with clients spanning the financial services, education and public sectors, utilizing AI to empower their operations and enhance their services.
In my early encounters with AI, I marveled at its potential to revolutionize industries. The ability to analyze vast data sets with lightning speed, provide insightful recommendations and automate complex processes was a game changer. We witnessed firsthand how AI-driven tools could transform customer engagement, optimize resource allocation and drive innovation.
However, with these remarkable advancements came an imperative to tread carefully. The financial sector, in particular, demanded a meticulous approach. We learned that harnessing the power of AI in finance required not only technical expertise but also a deep commitment to ethics. Bias in algorithmic lending, for instance, emerged as a critical concern. Our journey led us to invest significant resources in fine-tuning algorithms and rigorously scrutinizing data to ensure fairness and inclusivity in lending decisions.
Unlocking The Power Of AI And Automation
AI and automation are not just tools; they are catalysts for progress. They bring forth the promise of increased efficiency, precision and growth across diverse sectors. However, as we immerse ourselves in these innovations, we must not lose sight of the ethical compass that should always accompany our journey. Ethical AI signifies our commitment to developing, deploying and managing AI systems that prioritize fairness, transparency and accountability.
Addressing Bias: Fostering Fairness And Inclusivity
One of the most pressing challenges in the development of AI lies in the potential for bias within algorithms. These systems learn from historical data, and if that data carries hidden biases, AI may unwittingly perpetuate them. This can lead to biased decisions in critical areas such as hiring, lending and criminal justice. To combat this, organizations must undertake a diligent process of scrutiny, carefully examining training data to detect and rectify any potential biases.
Transparency And Accountability: Shining A Light On AI Decisions
Transparency is a fundamental pillar of ethical AI. As AI systems take on roles that influence people's lives, the ability to understand the reasoning behind their decisions becomes paramount. The concept of explainable AI has emerged, emphasizing the need for AI systems to provide clear explanations for their choices. Furthermore, accountability takes center stage. By establishing clear lines of responsibility for AI systems, we ensure that ethics remain at the forefront, with accountability resting in human hands.
Harmony In Collaboration: Humans And AI Together
Amid concerns about AI replacing human jobs, the true potential lies in a collaborative partnership. AI has the capacity to amplify human capabilities, freeing us to focus on tasks that require creativity, empathy and intricate decision-making. To harness this potential fully, organizations must adopt a people-centric approach, using AI to augment human capabilities and fostering collaboration that enhances productivity and innovation.
Navigating The Maze Of Regulations
As AI becomes an integral part of our daily lives, regulations must evolve to ensure ethical AI practices. Governments and institutions are crafting frameworks to address the ethical complexities entwined with AI. Staying informed about these regulations goes beyond mere compliance; it is essential for businesses to uphold ethical standards and navigate potential legal and reputational challenges.
Real Stories Of Ethical AI Success
In various sectors, pioneering organizations are demonstrating the impact of ethical AI. In healthcare, AI-powered diagnostic tools are facilitating more precise and timely medical assessments. Financial institutions are leveraging AI to detect fraud while minimizing false alarms. These real-world successes underscore the potential of AI when ethics guide its development.
Looking Forward: Ethical Considerations For Tomorrow
As AI continues to evolve, new ethical dilemmas emerge. The advent of autonomous vehicles, AI-assisted medical diagnoses, predictive analytics and more present novel challenges. Organizations must anticipate these complexities and proactively develop strategies to address them. By doing so, we can paint a vision of an AI-infused future that combines technological progress with ethical responsibility.
Ten Guidelines For Ethical AI Implementation
Ready to start harnessing ethical AI in your organization? Start with these first steps:
• Mitigating Bias: Regularly review and refine AI algorithms to reduce biases.
• Transparency Is Key: Ensure that AI decisions are transparent and comprehensible.
• Ownership And Responsibility: Clearly define roles and responsibilities for AI outcomes.
• Respect For Data Privacy: Safeguard user data and privacy in AI applications.
• Vigilance And Monitoring: Keep a watchful eye on AI systems for unexpected outcomes.
• Human Oversight: Incorporate human supervision in decisions with significant consequences.
• Educating Users: Inform users about AI's role and limitations in decision-making.
• Diverse Perspectives: Involve diverse teams in AI development for a range of insights.
• Adherence To Regulations: Stay informed about evolving AI-related regulations and ensure compliance.
• Promote Ethical Culture: Instill ethics training to empower employees for ethical AI engagement.
As we traverse the landscape of AI and automation, we must ensure that our journey is guided by ethical principles. By addressing bias, embracing transparency, navigating regulations and fostering collaboration between humans and AI, we unlock AI's potential while upholding the values that define us. It's a journey that combines technological innovation with ethical integrity, ultimately shaping a brighter future for all.

Examples include OpenAI's GPT-4, which can generate human-like text based on a given prompt, and tools like Runway and Artbreeder, which use AI to generate images and designs. As generative AI technology continues to advance, it is essential for businesses to stay informed and adapt.
However, it's important to note that while generative AI presents many opportunities, it's not without its challenges. For one, there's the concern of content uniqueness. Relying heavily on AI can sometimes lead to generic content, missing the unique voice or tone a brand wants to convey.
There's also the risk of AI-generated content lacking the deep context and understanding that human writers inherently bring. Bias in AI, driven by training data, can further lead to content that unintentionally perpetuates stereotypes or misinformation. Additionally, with growing concerns about data privacy, businesses must be cautious about where and how they source data for their AI models to maintain user trust.
Best Practices For Combining Generative AI And SEO
Identifying Content Gaps
Analyze your existing content to identify areas with potential gaps in information or topics. You can also look to your competitors to identify any missing elements. For example, if your content lacks information on "sustainable fashion," you can input this prompt into an AI like ChatGPT to generate relevant blog topics or article outlines.
Keeping Up With Trends
You can use Google Trends to see what topics are trending in your area. For example, if "zero-waste living" is a buzzword, generative AI can suggest content angles such as "Tips for Starting a Zero-Waste Lifestyle."
Leveraging Google Search Console Insights
Analyze data from Google Search Console Insights to identify top and trending queries related to your site. If Google Search Console indicates that users are frequently querying "benefits of solar energy" and your site ranks on page two for this, input the query into generative AI. It can then give you ideas for a comprehensive article or for enriching existing content with the aim of boosting your position closer to page one.
Embracing The Intersection Of Generative AI And SEO For A Competitive Edge
The potential impact of generative AI on the future of SEO is significant, as it offers new opportunities for businesses to create engaging, relevant and optimized content more efficiently.
Embracing the intersection of generative AI and SEO as a competitive advantage in the digital era requires a strategic approach that balances human creativity with automation, implements best practices and adapts to evolving trends.

title: Meet The Former Missile Engineer Who Made Billions Outsourcing Jobs — To The U.S.
text:
Raj Sardana’s little-known Innova Solutions has become one of the biggest IT staffing and services providers in the U.S. thanks to an aggressive strategy of buying up and gutting struggling competitors. But just as the new billionaire is enjoying the spoils of his success, could AI knock it all down?
By Jemima McEvoy, Forbes Staff
Raj Sardana appears in the aisle of the Innova Solutions corporate jet at New Jersey’s Teterboro Airport just past 9 a.m. After spending the weekend at a wedding in nearby Jersey City, the 63-year-old is flying to Minneapolis to visit the Mall of America, where he has an outpost of his fast-growing Georgia-based staffing and IT outsourcing firm. He’s joined by his wife of 37 years, Nita, and son Rajan, 28, both vice presidents at the company.
Tossing aside their Louis Vuitton luggage and sunglasses, the trio nestle into the plush, wood-framed seats of the $9.5 million Bombardier Global Express, purchased by Innova in 2020 as an upgrade to its previous Challenger 850, which Sardana points out was used in the first season of Netflix’s billionaire-focused soap opera, Dynasty. Once in the air, the family digs into plates of omelets, fruit and pastries served to them with golden knives and forks by an assistant who says she was hired two weeks prior.
“Did you see that?” Sardana says, grinning enthusiastically as he steps onto the tarmac of the non-commercial landing-area at the Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport about two and a half hours later, waving to the last two letters of the tail number painted in bright blue on the rear of the plane. “R.S.,” he reads aloud – he’s wearing matching cufflinks with the initials, “for Raj Sardana.”
Sardana, who came to the U.S. from India 42 years ago and started his company in 1998, is reveling in his newfound success. Over the past three years, Innova (known until recently as American CyberSystems or ACS) has muscled its way into the ranks of the U.S.’s top IT services firms. Revenue tripled to $2.4 billion in 2022, up from $860 million in 2020. Staffing Industry Analysts now ranks Innova as the No. 4 largest IT staffing company in the U.S., up from No. 19 in 2021.
Though it is much smaller and has a much lower profile than many of its publicly traded-competitors–such as Indian outsourcing giants Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro and Accenture, headquartered in Dublin, Ireland–more than 1,100 large and mid-sized companies, including Tesla, Harley Davidson, Verizon and Raytheon, rely on Innova’s pool of 55,000 predominantly U.S.-based contractors to build their apps, manage their data and staff a litany of other tech-related projects lasting anywhere from a few weeks to over a year.
Sardana owns the company with his wife Nita and is worth an estimated $2 billion (he claims the number is double that), making him one of the country’s most successful immigrant entrepreneurs. “This truly is a land of dreams,” says Sardana, who earlier this year splashed out $8.6 million for a 14-acre spread in Atlanta’s upscale Buckhead neighborhood, designed as a (much bigger) replica of Thomas Jefferson’s Monticello estate, replete with a life-size statue of a buck on its front lawn. “Yes, you have to work hard, but at least this country gives us an opportunity to get somewhere.”
It’s not easy to make it big in the overpopulated world of outsourcing, and Innova’s breakneck growth has mostly come from an aggressive acquisition strategy that has involved buying up struggling competitors with attractive clients (Tesla and Harley Davidson both came from acquisitions), and then cutting the “deadweight” from the inherited staff. It bought up six companies in 2021 and 2022, including New York-based staffing firm Diversant and publicly-traded Volt Information Sciences. As a result, only 41% of Innova’s growth during this period was organic.
While these deals boosted Innova’s top line, none has so far helped the bottomline. Volt, for instance, added $830 million in revenue but just $1 million in net profit and $60 million in debt. Innova’s net profits totaled just $65 million last year, translating to a tiny net margin of just 2.7%, well below Accenture, for instance, which netted 12%. Innova has about $370 million in net debt after these purchases. The ever-optimistic Sardana positions this as an opportunity to wring out profits from poorly run businesses. He’s projecting Innova’s revenue to surpass $3 billion this year and insisting that margins are on the rise (though he wouldn’t project net earnings for 2023). But there are plenty of signs that things may get tougher.
The so-called “rollup” strategy of buying up IT services competitors can be risky even in good times, explains Jeff Silber, an analyst who covers the industry for BMO Capital Markets. And these aren’t good times. Outsourcing giants like Tata Consultancy Services, Accenture, Infosys and Wipro have all slowed hiring or cut staff this year amid a slowdown in IT spending. The hiring decline could be the least of its worries, though, as advancements in generative AI threaten to upend the industry. It’s still unknown just how many jobs can be done by algorithms, but some of Innova’s competitors have already started to move aggressively to get ahead of the trend. Wipro earlier this month announced it will invest $1 billion over the next three years to build out its AI capabilities, including training its entire 250,000 person workforce in the technology, while Accenture bought the generative AI platform Writer in September.
Sardana believes that the company’s financial discipline will see it through this tricky macroeconomic landscape. “We are not at the edge where just a 10% revenue drop and we’re out of business,” he says. Plus he too is embracing AI. He says he’s cut down on human recruiters over the past two years (they still have 1,000, mostly based in India) and instead relies on AI to sift through its proprietary database of more than 15 million resumes scraped from the internet, including from job boards, and find the best candidates to match a job description. In 2022, Sardana personally spent $10 million (and pledged another $20 to $30 million over the next few years) to acquire a majority stake in Work Llama, an AI driven chatbot company that he says Innova uses to reach out to candidates and check their availability, qualifications and sometimes even conduct a short video interview. His hope is to help pitch it to other companies, too.
Regardless of how the industry reshapes, Sardana says he’s in it for the long haul. “He’s willing to bet pretty much everything, which a lot of people don’t,” says Sardana’s younger brother Sanjeev, the chief operating officer at Innova. He is one of five immediate family members to whom Sardana has given plum jobs at the company–his two daughters, Sonia and Shivani, are also VPs, in addition to his wife and son.
“People like me have some loose nut in the brain,” Sardana says, clarifying soon after: “I’m just joking.” But, he emphasizes: “These are calculated moves. I’m not stupid.”
Sardana traces his appetite for risk taking to “very, very humble” beginnings, starting with his childhood in New Delhi. His parents, both from Punjab, India, were forced to relocate to the country’s capital in the bloody aftermath of the 1947 partition of British India. The division of the former colonial territory into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan triggered one of the biggest refugee crises of the past century, displacing an estimated 15 million people, including Sardana’s parents, who fled their home after seeing some of their family members killed.
Rebuilding their lives in Delhi, Sardana’s father found work as a government administrator, his mother as a kindergarten teacher. Sardana, his brother Sanjeev and his parents shared a 225 square foot, one-bedroom apartment provided by the government, according to Sardana. As was quite common at the time, there was no heat, air conditioning or refrigerator. “This is in the ‘60s in India, so obviously the standards of living were different, amenities were different,” says Sanjeev, describing it as a “decent living” in a lower middle class family. “From the very beginning, the focus was on education to make sure you studied hard, you did well, so you could grow out of that situation.”
Sardana did just that. He graduated from a local engineering college and then moved to the U.S. in the early 1980s to get his masters in mechanical engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology. It was a big break, but by no means smooth sailing for Sardana, who says he arrived in Atlanta with “maybe a hundred dollars in my pocket” after scraping together the money for a plane ticket. “[I] started my life from scratch here,” he says. “I got a job at the cafeteria of Georgia Tech and supported myself through college.”
When he graduated, Sardana was hired by a supplier of Pratt & Whitney aircraft engine parts before eventually getting a job helping to make the turbine engines used to fire the Tomahawk missiles for a unit of defense contractor Teledyne. But in 1990, as the Cold War waned, Sardana and many of his colleagues were laid off. Fearful of his sudden lack of job security, Sardana struck out on his own, using $25,000 in savings to buy a print shop in Stone Mountain, Georgia. By 1997, he had built a small empire of two print shops, eight gas stations and two dry cleaning stores.
The cash flow from these businesses was enough that in 1998, Sardana was finally able to reenter the industry he was passionate about: technology. Seeing American companies fall into a frenzy over the much hyped Y2K scare (that’s when many experts predicted–wrongly, it turned out–that the transition from 1999 to 2000 would lead to widespread computer failures) he got the idea of recruiting programmers from India to help U.S. firms sift out the “Millennium Bug” in their systems. To get Innova off the ground, he and his brother flew to India and spent months interviewing 1,000 programmers before choosing 125 to sponsor for H1-B visas. In those days, the now much sought after visas were still gaining popularity and the government had recently increased its allotment. Despite his firm’s lack of name recognition, the talent shortage in the U.S. was so severe that the now-renamed American CyberSystems recorded $1 million in revenue its first year in business, according to Sardana.
Soon enough, though, the Y2K frenzy was over and Sardana was back where he started–until another national crisis struck. The September 11 terrorist attacks on the U.S. by Islamist extremist group Al Qaeda in 2001 spurred a surge in defense spending that Sardana figured he could tap. Leveraging his aerospace background, he began approaching major defense contractors like Northrop Grumman and Raytheon to supply much-needed engineering talent. This required transforming the business. “We went from an H1-B shop to a defense subcontractor just hiring U.S. citizens, and a lot of them had secret or top secret clearances,” says Sardana, who claims he personally gained top secret security clearance in 2004 (he became a citizen in 1990) after a two year assessment that involved the government visiting his family in India. (The Department Of Defense said it does not comment on any individual’s security clearance.)
Innova’s early growth was helped in part by its status as a minority-owned business, which Sardana says gave it an “extra edge” in securing government contracts and clients with vendor diversity quotas. But Sardana found a way to speed it up. Around the time of the 2008 financial crisis, he started buying a few small staffing firms with offshore presences in places like the Dominican Republic and India. Then, in 2012, just after Innova had hit about $100 million in sales, he made a bigger gamble, snapping up the staffing arm of Comforce, a once publicly traded company based in New York that had been bought for cheap – $85 million – by private equity firm ARBY Partners about two years prior. Comforce’s staffing business was doing about $170 million in revenues and ABRY, which only wanted to hold onto the managed service provider (MSP) part of the business, was willing to let it go for about $50 million. Innova had to borrow all the money for the deal from a group of banks including Bank of America and Fifth Third Bank, according to longtime Innova Chief Financial Officer Nick Goel, who says he was hired in 2005 as the firm’s controller after seeing a posting on Monster.com.
It was such a tough lift that Goel says he was shocked when, less than a year later, Sardana ordered him to go back to the same banks for more money for a second acquisition–this time to buy finance and engineering-focused staffing firm Analysts International. One of the original banks declined, citing overly fast growth. But two others said yes, and Goel rustled together loans for the $35 million deal.
Today, Innova sticks to a more conservative rule of thumb of buying companies whose cost it will be able to pay back within three years. Sardana says he leaves the acquired firm as is for about a year and then starts cutting the fat and moving core corporate operations overseas. In the case of Volt, its most recent major acquisition, Sardana says he inherited about 1,700 people but has cut that down to 1,000. “[Sardana’s] mantra has always been if your competitors can do it, we can do it better and cheaper,” says longtime Innova executive Brian Sonderholm, who is now Volt’s chief revenue officer, later correcting himself: “Don’t say cheaper… lower total cost of ownership.”
Still, one customer praised the level of customer service with Innova compared to other outsourcing firms. “They do a nice job. I’ve worked with some massive Indian firms and even though Raj is continuing to grow, he has kept a culture that understands how to execute as more of a boutique capability,” said Shawn Eads of PennEngineering, a Pennsylvania-based manufacturer that has worked with a mostly offshore team of Innova contractors since 2021 on a mix of IT staffing and services projects including architecting disaster recovery and data analytics and data strategy projects.
Sardana’s ties to India remain strong. In Noida, a city just outside New Delhi, Innova occupies a swanky eight-floor tower and a second smaller office nearby, where 2,400 employees – mostly in their 20s and 30s – work on tasks like HR, legal and IT infrastructure to support their clients’ projects. There’s a nine month training process before a new hire can be deployed on a project. Employees interviewed by Forbes on site praised Innova as a progressive work environment–at the time of the magazine’s visit, the office was decorated with Pride flags and offered complementary cab rides to make sure female employees could get home safely after late shifts. “We have a great work culture,” said Anisha Mehta, an HR specialist who highlighted that she’s been allowed to “move up the ladder quickly” in her four years at Innova.
Big “delivery centers” in lower-cost locations like Noida are crucial to Innova’s business model. While Sardana touts the fact that most of the firm’s contractors are located in the U.S., an attractive sell for clients wanting workers in the same time zone, about half of their corporate staff are based offshore. Innova has been building out its overseas presence, in India but also in Taiwan and Mexico, to handle more technical projects and product development, in an effort to extend its offerings beyond pure staffing. “You have to have more than just talent you’re offering,” Sardana says, explaining: “You can outsource this entire project to us and we’ll take care of it. That’s how we can see more sticky revenues.”
In contrast, Innova’s U.S. corporate presence seems much more modest. Outside of its headquarters, a nondescript red brick building in the Atlanta suburb of Duluth, the company previously listed 36 other offices across the country on its website. The company has since wiped seven of these offices from the site following questions from Forbes about an office listed in Gurnee, Illinois, which turned out to be a barn-like building with a note on the door alerting tenants that it was “not approved for occupancy. When asked about the Gurnee office, Sardana said Innova opened one there during the pandemic to service a nearby client, Abbott Labs, but he doesn’t think they have the location anymore. Other offices, he says, are kept mainly for client meetings and many were downsized during the pandemic because many of Innova’s employees now work remotely.
Innova’s cost-cutting ways have not always won it fans. Innova has been sued at least three times by former owners of companies it acquired. They’re all battling over relatively small sums—the latest is an ongoing lawsuit from the former owners of Diversant, who claim Innova owes them over $400,000 in tax refunds from prior to their December 2021 sale. None of these companies responded to inquiries from Forbes. (The firm also settled in May with the U.S. Department of Justice, paying a fine and agreeing to retrain staff, after violating the Immigration and Nationality Act with two job postings.)
Sardana blames at least two of the suits on what he describes as manipulative sellers. “We acquire companies that are not very well managed because that’s the way we get the best value… and then we apply our own business principles making good decisions to turn the trajectory around,” he says.
As for his contractors, the Innova Solutions CEO insists that his reliance on U.S.-based tech talent will insulate him from any cataclysmic shifts. “Companies that do a lot of grunt work will be impacted the most because AI will do all that grunt work, whether it’s research, whether it’s code generation,” says Sardana, pointing to competitors like Cognizant and Tata Consultancy Services with hundreds of thousands of India-based employees. “TCS has 300,000 employees in India doing mostly grunt work. Whereas, we have only 10,000 employees in India because most of our work is done here in the U.S.”
Taking a positive spin, Sardana is predicting “tremendous, tremendous” opportunities thanks to generative AI, which he says his staff are actively learning and figuring out how to implement with their clients. In any case, Sardana welcomes the opportunity for a challenge “Unless there’s something big and challenging, it’s boring,” he explains. “I mean we’re doing this mundane stuff every day, same old same old, is too boring. We need some excitement.”

title: Council Post: Service Intelligence 2.0: The Role Of LLMs In The Digital Era
text:
Amit Verma is the Founding Member and Head of Engineering at Neuron7.ai, a leader in Service Intelligence.
In today's digital era, service organizations across various industries are recognizing the importance of service intelligence, an approach that harnesses the power of data, analytics and AI to revolutionize service delivery.
Incumbents such as Salesforce and ServiceNow have announced their AI initiatives “Einstein for Service” and “Now Intelligence” respectively, to harness the power of AI and enable users to resolve issues efficiently by leveraging generative AI. This transformative concept is gaining momentum, and for good reason.
In this article, we delve into service intelligence, exploring its significance, its challenges and how it's driving the future of service optimization.
The Data Explosion
The digitalization of services has ushered in an era of unprecedented data generation. Organizations are flooded with vast volumes of data stemming from customer interactions, service operations and product performance. When effectively harnessed, this data can become a gold mine of insights. However, extracting value from such massive data sets is a Herculean task for traditional approaches.
Challenges At Scale
Organizations supporting a diverse array of products and models face a daunting challenge. With potentially thousands of product malfunctions and hundreds of thousands of resolution paths, the complexity exceeds human capacity. Information critical for issue resolution is scattered across knowledge base articles, product manuals, case notes, and experts' minds, and potentially siloed in different products within the organization.
A typical landscape can include a case management application (such as Salesforce or ServiceNow), a knowledge management system (such as Atlassian Confluence or Microsoft Sharepoint) and a connected device data analysis platform (like Splunk, Datadog and others). This fragmentation makes it arduous to promptly identify the best solution.
Global Complexity
Global service organizations face an added layer of complexity. Expertise is often geographically dispersed, and teams operate in diverse languages and often in different application stacks. Coordinating service intelligence efforts across borders necessitates advanced solutions.
Knowledge Erosion
Additionally, organizations grapple with knowledge erosion. As seasoned experts retire or move on, vital knowledge is at risk of being lost. New employees face a steep learning curve without access to comprehensive training and technology-driven information retrieval. As one article in Harvard Business Review points out, the “great resignation” didn’t start with the pandemic.
Evaluating Standard LLMs Versus Custom LLMs
AI—the linchpin of service intelligence—possesses the extraordinary capability to analyze colossal data sets, identify patterns, predict outcomes and continuously learn from new data. However, not all AI is created equal.
A quick look into Meta’s AI LLaMA paper shows that the bulk of the training data for LLMs is a mix of CommonCrawl, Wikipedia, StackExchange and other publicly sourced data. Standard large language models (LLMs) are not specifically fine-tuned for domain-specific tasks or tailored to understand the unique language used within the context of the organization.
Custom LLMs may address these challenges by being fine-tuned on domain-specific data. They can also align more closely with the requirements and nuances of service intelligence, making them a better fit for specialized fields. Organizations interested in pursuing an LLM solution should consider the following aspects to determine if standard LLMs would address their needs or if they should consider custom LLMs.
Domain Specificity
Service intelligence often operates within specialized domains like healthcare, finance or manufacturing. Standard LLMs are typically trained on general internet text, meaning they may lack domain-specific knowledge. For instance, differentiating between "MRI machine" and "magnetic resonance imaging device" could be challenging.
Custom LLMs, fine-tuned for specific domains, help bridge this knowledge gap, enabling the precise understanding and processing of service-related content. Developing test cases that accurately represent the organization's domain and evaluating performance against these cases empowers the user to make an informed choice whether to use standard LLMs or train custom LLMs.
Data Privacy And Security Compliance
In service intelligence, handling sensitive customer data and proprietary information is commonplace. Standard LLMs are not inherently equipped to meet the data privacy and security requirements inherent in various industries. Custom LLMs can be trained to recognize and classify sensitive information, such as personally identifiable information (PII), financial data or proprietary information.
When choosing between standard and custom LLMs, determine the level of sensitivity of the data your organization deals with and complement the approach with additional security measures, such as data anonymization, access controls and encryption to safeguard sensitive information.
Contextual Mastery
Service interactions demand a deep understanding of context. Standard LLMs may not fully grasp the intricacies and nuances of service-related conversations, leading to inaccuracies in responses and recommendations.
For example, the issue “signal analyzer is not working” for a high-tech manufacturer may refer to a particular product model that the standard LLMs cannot disambiguate. Custom LLMs, trained with context-specific data, excel in providing accurate and context-aware solutions.
To make an informed choice, it's vital to delineate your contextual needs, evaluate the accuracy of standard LLMs in context and assess the availability of context-specific data for training custom LLMs.
Integration With Knowledge Bases
Organizations maintain repositories of service-specific knowledge in the form of knowledge bases and documentation. Standard LLMs may not integrate seamlessly with these knowledge bases and may fail to provide a resolution path. For example, “How do you debug a LO failure for E7541A” and “Low Order issue on spectrum analyzer” may refer to the same resolution path from the same service manual. Custom LLMs can be tailored for this context-aware natural language querying.
It's crucial to note that custom LLMs require consistent updates to remain pertinent as knowledge bases evolve. This underscores the importance of robust data governance and routine model assessment to ensure the optimal choice between standard and custom LLMs.
Final Thoughts
I believe that service intelligence, driven by AI and LLMs, stands at the forefront of service optimization. When approached successfully, it can help empower organizations to unlock the full potential of their data, streamline operations, ensure compliance and enhance customer experiences.

title: Council Post: Three Questions To Ask Yourself Before Launching A Generative AI Project
text:
Elise Carmichael is the CTO of Lakeside Software, where she oversees the design and delivery of its digital employee experience platform.
As the CTO of a software company, I, like many of my peers, have found myself engrossed by generative large language models ever since OpenAI's release of the GPT-3 model in 2020.
With eyes glued to Microsoft's ongoing developments in deep engagement and Copilots, I can only imagine the power of these models when trained on even more data. If we’ve learned one big thing from these models, it is that more data is better—and significantly so.
Of course, with ChatGPT being so accessible, one of the first frivolous things I asked ChatGPT was to create a haiku to market my company’s flagship product. Keeping up the fun, I asked it to describe my company in various formats: a news segment, a police report, a sonnet.
Yes, I went down the same rabbit hole as everyone else. While playing with any shiny, new object in the tech world, though, we owe it to our collective contributions to innovation to ask, "What can I do with this?"
Fortunately, most companies are asking that same question. A recent KPMG survey of executives revealed, "71 percent plan to implement their first generative AI solution within two years" (pg. 1). There hasn’t been this much buzz since the digital transformations and huge cloud migrations of a decade ago.
OpenAI's ChatGPT may be the app that launched the frenzy, but that’s because it has democratized access to powerfully trained GPT (generative pre-trained transformer) models. OpenAI created the first GPT in 2018—and it was really a game changer then. Over the past five years, OpenAI has trained new models (like GPT-3 and GPT-4) on more and more data.
Data is the main driving factor here, making the models faster and more accurate.
Before ideating and investing in your own generative AI project, I suggest approaching the project just as you would with any other visionary tech. Otherwise, your generative AI project may be destined to fall flat like any number of "great" failed inventions on display at the Museum of Failure.
More specifically, I suggest asking yourself the following questions.
1. Is our data house in order?
Any generative AI system or integration will be only as good as the data feeding it. This catch may present the biggest challenge for most enterprises keen on creating their own models. Developing a solid data strategy, including clear data governance, should be the first step. Don’t put the AI cart before the data horse.
Why is this step so crucial? At present, large language models rely primarily on information from the internet (a.k.a. sometimes the Wild West). Much of that new data will be created by large language models. Bots feeding bots feeding bots feels like a bad cycle. Because these models are only as good as their data, they inherently have biases and cases of misinformation.
Part of this scenario is the data; another part is that these models are not "smart." They fundamentally are guessing the next word in a sentence based on the previous words, so you don’t get the same response every time. They mix up the probability of what the next word will be. For example, "The sky is (fill in the blank)"—is it blue? Is it falling? It will take a guess and continue on from there.
Look within—and use human expertise—to find a solution to this problem. Is your enterprise sitting on data that can enable a more competitive, domain-specific generative AI system?
2. Which specific problem are we trying to solve?
As with any technological advancement, a specific use case must be the starting point, not an afterthought—ultimately delivering concrete value. Ask, "What is the specific problem we are solving?"
You don’t have to go all in at once, nor should you. A pilot use case or two is essential. And remember, although ChatGPT is impressive, it may not be the best fit in all scenarios.
We’re just scratching the surface of generative AI’s realistic use cases. I am a firm believer that generative AI can become a trusty teammate that helps boost your productivity. In my own day-to-day, I use GitHub Copilot. No, it’s not perfect. But if you want to have an assistant help you write unit tests, figure out what the syntax for the "main" function looks like in Java or all the other things you know you look for on Stack Overflow, it’s in the IDE with you at all times. In this regard, generative AI is a great way to augment initial tasks.
3. What business outcomes can we realize?
Once you’ve identified strong use cases, ask yourself, "What are the measurable business outcomes I want to achieve for my company? For my targeted customers?"
I suggest looking to your core business for answers. Don’t try to fix what’s not broken; instead, consider whether generative AI can make your processes and/or products better and, if so, how.
In my industry (digital employee experience, or DEX), for instance, we are committed to empowering IT teams to adopt a proactive approach instead of the traditional reactive one. One element of a DEX strategy is reducing the mean time to resolution (MTTR) whenever an employee opens an IT ticket. We have strong customer-proof points for reducing MTTR. So our guiding question is, "Can integrating a generative AI model cut MTTR more by automating certain tasks?"
Are you ready to begin?
It’s understandable that most companies want a piece of the generative AI pie, which "attracted more than $1.37 billion venture capital dollars in 2022" (pg. 3 of the KPMG report).
All CTOs, CIOs, CMOs and CFOs (get me?) are weighing the possibilities for their own use cases. It's crucial to recognize that generative AI systems are evolving fast. What will the regulatory landscape look like this time next year? Let’s ask ChatGPT.

title: Council Post: What Generative AI Can Mean For Enterprises
text:
Rajat Sharma, SVP and Global Head of Technology Ecosystem and Growth for Zensar Technologies.
On one side, business leaders today must contend with the power play between increasing interest rates, inflation and geopolitical tensions. On the other side, they have to watch the latest and greatest technologies accelerate the creation of new products and services.
One of these technologies that has been recently discovered is generative AI (GenAI). Yes, I am using the word "discovered," not invented, as generative AI has been in existence for many years. However, it was uncovered for mass adoption when OpenAI released ChatGPT in November 2022.
In this article, I will not delve into the details of what GenAI is, as many other publications have written on this topic. Instead, I will explain what I believe has become possible beyond the previously widely available AI models, which offered use cases ranging from sentiment analysis to analyzing business indicators to offering recommendations.
What GenAI brings to the table is the capability of not only scanning, analyzing and learning from large amounts of data sets and creating predictions but also the ability to infuse the expertise of “structuring” and “storyboarding” in the same manner as a mature professional. This is all done based on the accuracy of prompts that users provide—that is, “prompt engineering”—to continuously train large language models (LLMs).
With this in mind, let's look at how enterprises can leverage GenAI at scale:
Corporate Systems
GenAI can and should be leveraged across the corporate systems. This includes everything from sourcing to customer relationship management (CRM) to product and service delivery, including enterprise resource planning (ERP) and corporate functions like finance, planning, reporting, HR, sales and regulatory compliance.
Consider the supply chain. GenAI can be very effective and efficient in functions that are high on documented contents and SOP-based delivery, like customer care or intensive data processing functions. But it can also optimize the supply chain to work on just-in-time inventory by providing visibility and predictions about the consumption of resources across warehouses, stores and in-transit to create a structured output of how the inventory needs to be managed at a point in time.
To do that, you need to make the right data sets—called vector databases—for running GenAI models. Vector databases, however, will require extensive and continued consumption of cloud resources—not just cloud ML/GenAI functions, but more computing, storage and network capacity as well as GPUs to run LLMs.
Product and Services Development
In today’s API economy, every product and application is a software product. Even if it is a physical product, it is more than likely still driven by software or is enhanced to integrate with software. The core business of every enterprise, therefore, is either to develop products or services or to improve existing products. Here's how GenAI can help with those two goals:
1. GenAI can be infused across the development value chain from ideation (which is heavy on research and content creation) to requirements (which requires structuring to avoid gaps between the business and technology) to core development and testing (which McKinsey has explained well in their article, "Unleash Developer Productivity With Generative AI").
2. Since all products are software products, look for ways that GenAI can enhance the capabilities and features of existing products. For example, Google recently added Duet to their Workspace product line, which can enhance the workplace as an assistant in ways like creating summaries from meetings or attending meetings on behalf of users.
IT And OT Processes, Policies And Governance
Automation first revolutionized many IT processes: service management, controls, governance and integration into DevSecOps. IT operations (ITOps) then transformed siloed applications, infrastructure, data and security operations into a more integrated cloud operations model, incorporating the principles of site reliability engineering (SRE) value chain.
ITOps is now evolving into AIOps, where AI and automation are infused into every area of operations, from asset inventory and monitoring to log aggregation/analytics and feedback for reliable, scalable and composable operations.
The next step will likely be GenAI leveraging the generative capabilities across the “east-west” (from user experience to workload management) and "north-south" (from managing applications—microservices/APIs—to cloud infrastructure, networks, security and data).
Consider how this could impact mature and highly automated service desk operations by structuring even the most complex and ever-evolving SOPs to resolve advanced problems and bug fixing across infrastructure, apps, security and data in an agile and composable enterprise. Similarly, with network operations (NOC)/security operations (SOC)/IoT operations, it will continue to learn and structure alerts, alarms, traces, event data and their correlations, but it will also start writing the infrastructure code for configurations which could lead to innovative, self-healing platforms.
In order for these outcomes to be achieved, however, GenAI will need to evolve with more standardization, safety, bias mitigation, security, economy and governance. Once it does, GenAI plays a more active role in governing enterprise GenAI through continuous learning of policies, spending and governing patterns.
The enterprise of tomorrow should not just look at independent and isolated GenAI use cases but look at this as an enterprise initiative from systems of engagements (front office/client-side) to systems of records (back office/supply side), including products and operations. This can lead to the emergence of “systems of generative intelligence” in order to create a "generative enterprise."
